concepts.title: Why Clicking Through the Console Doesn't Scale
concepts.description: Making a change directly in the AWS console, often called ClickOps, is fast and fine for one person exploring or prototyping, but it leaves no diff to review, no reliable record of why a value changed, and no guarantee that two 'identical' environments stay identical. Knowing what breaks, and when, is the motivation for everything Infrastructure as Code fixes.
learningObjectives: Explain what 'ClickOps' means and why manual console changes are hard to reproduce exactly across environments or people.
Explain configuration drift and how it accumulates when infrastructure changes aren't tracked in a single, shared source of truth.
Explain why manual changes are harder to review, audit, and roll back than changes expressed as versioned code.
Explain what CloudTrail does and does not provide: it records that a change happened but is not a substitute for reviewing a change before it takes effect.
Identify legitimate, narrow uses of the console (exploration, learning, break-glass emergency access) and the discipline needed to keep those from becoming permanent drift unnoticed.

sections.heading: ClickOps: Fast for One Person, One Time
sections.body:
The AWS console is a good tool for one kind of situation: a single person exploring what a service does, prototyping a one-off idea, or learning how options fit together. Clicking through a wizard to launch an EC2 instance or create an S3 bucket gives immediate visual feedback, shows default values and inline explanations, and needs no setup beyond logging in. That is why earlier concepts in this course used the console for walkthroughs.

The trouble starts when a console change stops being exploratory and becomes how a real environment's configuration gets decided, which is **ClickOps**. The console has no concept of a definitive record of how an environment should be configured; it shows the current live state and lets you change it. No file captures *why* a security group rule was widened, nothing forces a second person to look at the change before it takes effect, and nothing stops the same change from being made three slightly different ways by three people in three environments weeks apart, each clicking from memory instead of following one authoritative recipe.

sections.heading: Configuration Drift: When Reality Diverges From Any Single Source of Truth
sections.body:
**Configuration drift** is what happens when two things that are supposed to be the same (two environments like staging and production, or a live resource and the template that created it) gradually diverge, usually without anyone deciding that they should. A common path: during a production incident, an engineer opens the console and widens a security group rule, bumps an instance size, or changes a timeout to resolve the emergency. The fix works, the incident ends, and, understandably, nobody goes back to make the same change in staging or to update the template that was supposed to describe production. Three months and several more emergency tweaks later, staging and production are no longer comparable, though everyone still talks about them as if they were.

This is the mechanism behind the common bug category 'it works in staging but breaks in production' (or the reverse): the application code is the same, but the *infrastructure* underneath has diverged in ways nobody working on the incident can see at a glance. Drift doesn't require carelessness. It follows from having several independently changeable copies of 'the same' environment and no single maintained source of truth that every change must flow through.

sections.heading: No Review, No Audit Trail, No Easy Rollback
sections.body:
Contrast a console change with a change expressed as code in a pull request. The code change has a diff: a reviewer sees what is added, removed, or modified before any of it takes effect, and can ask questions or block it. It has a commit history with an author, a timestamp, and ideally a message explaining why. Reverting is one well-understood operation, because the previous state was itself recorded as code and not just as whatever the console displayed a moment before someone clicked.

A console change has none of these properties. There is nothing to review, because the click *is* the change. There is no structured record of intent beyond whatever the engineer writes in a chat message or ticket, which is easy to skip under pressure and to lose later. And reverting needs someone to remember or reconstruct the previous configuration, which may never have been written down before it was overwritten. **CloudTrail** helps with part of this: it logs every console action that calls an AWS API, recording who made the call, when, and with what parameters, which is valuable forensic history, especially for security investigations. But CloudTrail records what *did* happen. It does not *review* a change before it happens, and reconstructing a resource's full configuration just before one event from a stream of API log entries is far more laborious than reading a two-line diff in a pull request.

sections.heading: Where the Console Still Makes Sense, and the Discipline That Keeps It From Becoming Drift
sections.body:
None of this means the console should never be touched once an environment exists. Exploration and learning are still what it is good for, and a **break-glass** scenario, an incident severe enough that the normal review-and-deploy pipeline is unavailable or too slow, is a reasonable narrow exception where a direct console change is the right call, not a process failure. The discipline that keeps it from becoming permanent, untracked drift is easy to state and easy to skip under pressure: **any emergency console change gets backported into the infrastructure-as-code source of truth immediately afterward**, as its own reviewed change. That way the next deploy of the environment doesn't undo the emergency fix, and every other environment that should match can be updated on purpose instead of by accident three months later.

A zero-exceptions rule ('nobody touches the console, ever') tends to be one people route around during a real emergency anyway. The more durable version keeps console access available for break-glass situations, with an explicit, non-optional follow-up step. Skipping the follow-up is the failure, not the emergency click.

examples.title: The Same Security Group Change, Two Ways
examples.code:
Console way:
  1. Open EC2 console -> Security Groups -> select 'app-sg'
  2. Click 'Edit inbound rules'
  3. Click 'Add rule', type 443, select 'Anywhere-IPv4', click 'Save rules'
  (no record of why, no review step, no diff -- the change simply takes effect)

Code way (a snippet of the underlying template):
  - Type: AWS::EC2::SecurityGroupIngress
    Properties:
      GroupId: !Ref AppSecurityGroup
      IpProtocol: tcp
      FromPort: 443
      ToPort: 443
      CidrIp: 0.0.0.0/0
  # proposed via a pull request, with a diff, a reviewer, and a commit message
  # explaining why 443 needed to be opened
examples.explanation: Both produce the same live outcome: port 443 open to the internet on this security group. The difference is what surrounds the change. The console sequence leaves only a CloudTrail entry recording that an `AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress` call happened, by a specific IAM principal at a specific time. That is useful afterward, but nobody reviewed the change before it took effect, and nothing explains why 443 needed to open beyond whatever the engineer mentioned elsewhere. The code version has a diff a reviewer sees before it is applied, a commit message with the reasoning, and a permanent record that is easy to revert: reverting the commit and reapplying removes this change and nothing else, with no need to remember what the group looked like before. (Opening 443 to `0.0.0.0/0` is normal for a public web tier and wrong for most internal services, so a reviewer's first question is who the rule is for.)

examples.title: CloudFormation Drift Detection Catching a Manual Console Change
examples.code:
aws cloudformation detect-stack-drift --stack-name app-network-stack

# drift detection is asynchronous: wait for it to finish with
#   aws cloudformation describe-stack-drift-detection-status --stack-drift-detection-id <id>
# then list the drifted resources:
aws cloudformation describe-stack-resource-drifts \
  --stack-name app-network-stack \
  --query "StackResourceDrifts[?StackResourceDriftStatus=='MODIFIED']"

# example result (abbreviated)
[
  {
    "LogicalResourceId": "AppSecurityGroup",
    "StackResourceDriftStatus": "MODIFIED",
    "PropertyDifferences": [
      { "PropertyPath": "/SecurityGroupIngress/1/CidrIp", "ExpectedValue": "10.0.0.0/16", "ActualValue": "0.0.0.0/0", "DifferenceType": "NOT_EQUAL" }
    ]
  }
]
examples.explanation: `detect-stack-drift` asks CloudFormation to compare each resource in the stack against what the template specifies instead of trusting that reality still matches. (Not every resource type supports drift detection; the ones that don't show as not checked.) The result shows one resource, `AppSecurityGroup`, flagged `MODIFIED`, with one ingress rule's `CidrIp` showing an `ExpectedValue` of `10.0.0.0/16` (an internal range, presumably what the template says) against an `ActualValue` of `0.0.0.0/0` (the whole internet). That is likely the residue of an emergency console widening like the one described earlier, made after the last deploy and never backported. Drift detection doesn't fix anything automatically. It surfaces the discrepancy so a human can decide whether to update the template to match a possibly still-needed change or redeploy to force reality back to the template, turning an invisible divergence into a decision made on purpose.

examples.title: A CloudTrail Event Shows What Happened, Not the Full Before/After Picture
examples.explanation: This event gives specific facts: at 02:14 UTC, someone who assumed the `OnCallEngineer` role (the session name, `j.smith`, identifies the person) called `AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress` on `sg-0abc123456789`, adding a rule that opens port 443 to `0.0.0.0/0`. It does not tell you, without correlating many other events, what every other rule on the group looked like just before the call, whether this was the first such change or the fifth, or why it was made. CloudTrail records API calls, not intent or before-and-after snapshots. Reconstructing the group's full rule set at 02:13 from CloudTrail alone means finding and replaying every earlier modifying event for that resource in order, the kind of forensic work a two-line diff in a pull request makes unnecessary. (This event is simplified from a real CloudTrail record, which has many more fields.)

misconceptions.description: CloudTrail logging means we already have full change-tracking and accountability, so infrastructure as code doesn't add much on top of that.
misconceptions.clarification: CloudTrail records that an API call was made, by whom, and with what parameters, which is valuable forensic history, especially for security investigations. It does not provide a pre-change review step, a readable diff of a resource's configuration before and after a change, or a guaranteed rollback to a known-good state. Reconstructing 'what changed and why' from CloudTrail events is much harder than reading a version-controlled diff that was reviewed before it took effect.
misconceptions.fact: CloudTrail records that an API call was made, by whom, and with what parameters -- valuable forensic history after the fact, especially for security investigations.

misconceptions.description: Configuration drift only happens when someone makes a careless mistake in the console; a careful, experienced engineer making a console change won't cause drift.
misconceptions.clarification: Drift accumulates just as easily from a correct, deliberate change, most commonly an emergency production fix made in the console during an incident, that never gets propagated to other environments or backported into the shared source of truth. It follows from having multiple independently changeable copies of 'the same' environment without a maintained source of truth, not from anyone doing something careless.

exercises.prompt: Given this CloudFormation drift-detection result, explain in plain terms what change was made outside of CloudFormation, and what specific risk it introduces if left unaddressed.
hints: ExpectedValue reflects what the CloudFormation template currently specifies; ActualValue reflects the resource's real, live configuration right now.
Think about what a BackupRetentionPeriod of 0, specifically, means for an RDS instance's automated backups.

Consider what would happen to this property the next time the stack is updated or redeployed from the template as it currently stands, versus what would happen if the incident that caused this change is forgotten.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Someone changed the RDS instance's automated backup retention from 7 days (what the template specifies) down to 0 (disabled) directly outside of CloudFormation -- likely to work around some issue during an incident, such as backup-related I/O contention. Left unaddressed, this means the database currently has no automated backups at all, a serious data-loss risk that isn't visible unless someone specifically runs drift detection, since the live database otherwise appears to be working fine.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The drift result isolates exactly one property difference: `BackupRetentionPeriod` is `7` in the template but `0` on the live resource, meaning automated backups have been disabled on the actual database even though the template -- the presumed source of truth -- still says they should be running with a 7-day retention window. This is a specific, serious instance of the general drift risk: unlike a cosmetic setting, a disabled backup silently removes a safety net that nobody would necessarily notice is missing until the moment a backup is actually needed and isn't there. The fix requires a human decision, not just an automated one: either this change was a deliberate, temporary workaround that should be reverted immediately by redeploying the template (restoring backups), or there's a real reason backups needed to be disabled, in which case the template itself should be updated to reflect that decision explicitly and reviewably, rather than leaving the live database quietly diverged from what anyone reading the template would assume is true.

exercises.prompt: During a production incident, an engineer widened a security group rule directly in the console to unblock traffic from a partner's new IP range, and the incident was resolved. Two months later, a CloudFormation stack update that changed the security group's ingress rules reset the rule to the template's original, narrower range, breaking the partner integration again with no obvious cause. Diagnose what process step was missing and describe the fix.
exercises.code:
// The security group's CloudFormation template, unchanged since before the incident:
SecurityGroupIngress:
  - IpProtocol: tcp
    FromPort: 443
    ToPort: 443
    CidrIp: 203.0.113.0/24   # partner's OLD IP range -- never updated after the incident

// The live security group's actual rule at the time of the incident fix (added via console, not reflected above):
#   FromPort: 443, ToPort: 443, CidrIp: 198.51.100.0/24   (partner's NEW range)
hints: Compare what the template says the rule should be against what was actually configured live during the incident -- were those two ever reconciled?
Think about what a CloudFormation stack update does to a property it has to change when the template was never updated to reflect the emergency change.
The fix isn't just 'redo the console change again' -- what step, done right after the incident, would have prevented this exact recurrence two months later?
exercises.solutionCode:
SecurityGroupIngress:
  - IpProtocol: tcp
    FromPort: 443
    ToPort: 443
    CidrIp: 198.51.100.0/24   # updated to match the partner's actual current range,
                              # backported into the template right after the incident,
                              # not left as an un-tracked console-only change
exercises.solutionExplanation: The missing step was backporting the emergency console change into the CloudFormation template right after the incident. The template still described the partner's old IP range as the source of truth, while the live security group had drifted to the correct new range through the console. Two months later a stack update touched the security group's ingress rules, and CloudFormation applied the template's outdated definition, overwriting the emergency fix nobody had recorded as permanent. (CloudFormation only changes resources whose template properties changed, so drift can sit unnoticed for months until an update happens to touch that property, which is what makes it a delayed regression.) The fix is to update the template's `CidrIp` to the partner's current range as a reviewed change right after the incident, so the next update reinforces the correct configuration. That is the 'backport immediately' discipline that keeps a legitimate break-glass change from becoming a time-delayed regression.

assessments.prompt: A team wants a reliable way to catch cases where someone changed a resource directly in the console instead of through their CloudFormation templates. Which approach most directly addresses this?
options: Reviewing CloudTrail logs manually once a quarter for any API calls that look suspicious, then asking each engineer to explain any change they made outside the normal process.
Running CloudFormation drift detection periodically (or on a schedule) and reviewing any resources flagged as MODIFIED against their template definitions.
Requiring every engineer to sign a policy promising not to use the console for changes.
Enabling MFA on all IAM users so console changes require an extra authentication step.
assessments.explanation: Drift detection is built for this question: it compares each stack resource's live configuration against what its template specifies and flags any discrepancy, which answers 'did this resource change outside of CloudFormation'. Manually reviewing CloudTrail logs (“Reviewing CloudTrail logs manually once a quarter…”) can theoretically surface the same information but requires correlating individual API events into a full picture of what changed, and doing it quarterly means drift could go unnoticed for months. A policy promising not to use the console (“Requiring every engineer to sign a policy…”) addresses intent, not detection, and doesn't catch anything that already happened, including legitimate break-glass changes that were never backported. MFA (“Enabling MFA on all IAM users…”) is a valuable security control but has nothing to do with detecting configuration drift -- it makes console access more secure, not more visible after the fact.

assessments.prompt: A careful, experienced engineer makes a deliberate, well-reasoned emergency change directly in the console during a production incident, intending to fix the problem quickly and correctly. Does this risk causing configuration drift?
options: No, because drift only results from careless mistakes, never from a deliberate, well-reasoned change made by an experienced engineer.
No, because CloudTrail automatically records the change and keeps every environment synchronized as a result.
Yes, but only if the engineer used the console instead of the AWS CLI to make the change.

Yes -- drift can accumulate from a correct, deliberate change just as easily as a careless one, if that change is never propagated to other environments or backported into the shared source of truth afterward; it's a structural consequence of having multiple independently-changeable copies of an environment, not a symptom of carelessness.
assessments.explanation: Drift doesn't require anyone to do anything wrong or careless -- the most common real path into it is exactly a correct, deliberate emergency fix that resolves the immediate problem but is never backported into the shared source of truth or propagated to other environments afterward. The “No, because drift only results from careless…” option incorrectly ties drift to carelessness specifically. The “No, because CloudTrail automatically records the change…” option misattributes a synchronization capability to CloudTrail, which only records that an API call happened -- it has no mechanism for keeping environments in sync with each other. The “Yes, but only if the engineer used…” option draws an arbitrary distinction between console and CLI changes; either could cause the same drift if never backported, since the risk comes from the change being untracked in the shared source of truth, not from which interface was used to make it.

assessments.prompt: A team believes that because CloudTrail logs every console action, they already have everything infrastructure-as-code would give them in terms of change tracking and review. What is missing from this reasoning?
options: CloudTrail records that an API call happened, by whom, and with what parameters -- valuable forensic history after the fact -- but it provides no pre-change review step, no readable diff of a resource's full before/after configuration, and no guaranteed simple rollback to a known-good prior state.
CloudTrail is disabled by default in every AWS account, so this reasoning doesn't even apply until it's explicitly turned on.
Nothing; CloudTrail's logging is functionally equivalent to a full code-review process.
CloudTrail only logs actions taken through the console, not API calls made via the CLI or SDKs, so it actually provides even less coverage than assumed.
assessments.explanation: CloudTrail's real value is forensic -- a record of what already happened -- not a substitute for the properties infrastructure-as-code provides: a diff reviewed before the change takes effect, a structured record of intent, and a reliable, exact rollback. The “Nothing; CloudTrail's logging is functionally equivalent…” option overstates CloudTrail's role entirely. The “CloudTrail only logs actions taken through…” option is factually wrong -- CloudTrail logs API calls regardless of whether they originated from the console, the CLI, or an SDK; it doesn't selectively cover only console actions. The “CloudTrail is disabled by default in every…” option is also wrong: every account has CloudTrail Event history on by default, recording management events for the last 90 days. You create a trail only to keep records longer or to deliver them to S3.

assessments.prompt: A team adopts a strict policy: console access is never allowed under any circumstances, with zero exceptions, even during a severe incident where the normal deploy pipeline itself is unavailable. What is the likely practical consequence of this zero-exceptions policy?
options: It has no real practical consequence, since a severe incident that makes the deploy pipeline unavailable is not a scenario worth planning for.
It makes CloudTrail logging unnecessary, since no console changes will ever occur to log.
It tends to produce exactly the kind of rule people quietly route around during a genuine emergency anyway.
It eliminates all risk of configuration drift entirely, since the console is never touched under any circumstances.
assessments.explanation: An absolute, zero-exceptions rule ignores that a severe enough incident can make the normal pipeline genuinely unavailable or too slow to help, and in that moment, someone facing real pressure to restore service is likely to reach for the console anyway, rule or no rule -- just now doing so quietly, without the structured backporting discipline a more realistic policy would have built in. The “It eliminates all risk of configuration drift…” option assumes perfect compliance under all circumstances, which the reasoning specifically argues against. The “It has no real practical consequence, since…” option dismisses a real operational scenario that does need planning for. The “It makes CloudTrail logging unnecessary, since…” option is a non-sequitur -- console changes can still happen under this policy in practice, and CloudTrail's value is independent of any specific console-access policy.

assessments.prompt: A junior engineer asks why their team insists on making infrastructure changes through code and pull requests instead of just clicking through the console, since the console change would be faster and produce the exact same end result. Explain the reasoning, including what CloudTrail does and doesn't solve.
assessments.modelAnswer: The console and a code-based change can produce an identical end state. The difference is what surrounds the change. A console change has no review step: nobody sees a diff of what is about to change, so mistakes and overly broad grants are caught after the fact, if at all, instead of by a second pair of eyes beforehand. A code change proposed as a pull request has that review step plus a permanent record of intent, a commit message tied to the diff instead of a chat message that gets lost. Reverting is the other gap: reverting a merged commit restores the previous state, because that state was recorded as code, while undoing a console change needs someone to remember what the configuration was, with no guarantee it was written down. CloudTrail is often assumed to close this gap alone. It does record that a console change happened, by whom, and with what parameters, which is valuable forensic history. But it provides no pre-change review, since the change has already taken effect by the time anyone reads the entry, and rebuilding a resource's prior configuration from individual API events is far more laborious than reading a two-line diff. At team scale, code is also what keeps dev, staging, and production comparable: the same reviewed template is applied to each, not three console recipes remembered separately. Console changes have no mechanism for staying in sync across environments, which is how drift accumulates.

concepts.title: CloudFormation and CDK: Declarative, Versioned Infrastructure
concepts.description: CloudFormation lets you describe the infrastructure you want as a template and leaves AWS to work out how to get there, in the right order. CDK layers a real programming language on top of the same engine, but neither replaces the discipline of reviewing a change set before you execute it.
learningObjectives: Explain what 'declarative' infrastructure means, contrasted with an imperative script that issues a fixed sequence of API calls.
Read a CloudFormation template's core anatomy -- Resources, Parameters, Outputs -- and explain how a logical ID relates to the actual physical resource it produces.
Explain what a stack is, and how CloudFormation reconciles a template against a stack's current state rather than blindly re-running commands.
Explain what a change set is and why reviewing one before executing an update is the CloudFormation-native equivalent of reviewing a code diff before merging.
Explain what AWS CDK adds on top of CloudFormation, and that cdk deploy synthesizes a template and still drives the same stack and change-set machinery underneath.
Identify common CloudFormation mistakes: missing DeletionPolicy on stateful resources, hardcoded account-specific values, and property changes that force resource replacement.

sections.heading: Declarative vs Imperative: Describing the End State, Not Scripting the Steps
sections.body:
A CloudFormation template is **declarative**: it describes the infrastructure you want to exist, and CloudFormation works out the sequence of create, update, and delete API calls needed to make reality match, including dependency ordering. A subnet must exist before an instance can launch into it, and CloudFormation infers that from the references between resources. Contrast an **imperative** shell script that calls `aws ec2 run-instances`, then `aws elbv2 create-load-balancer`, then wires them together with more commands in an order someone wrote by hand. The script describes a sequence of *actions*, not a desired *end state*. Running it twice compares nothing to what exists. It repeats the create calls, which usually means an error (the name already exists) or, worse, a duplicate set of resources.

A declarative template is safe to apply repeatedly: CloudFormation compares the template against the stack's tracked state, computes what differs, and does nothing if nothing changed. Reapplying an unchanged template is a no-op, which makes declarative infrastructure reliable to automate and rerun, unlike an imperative script that whoever wrote it must keep correct and idempotent by hand. (The comparison is against the previous *template*, not the live resource. That is why changes made outside CloudFormation go unnoticed until drift detection or an update touches them.)

sections.heading: Anatomy of a Template: Resources, Parameters, and Outputs
sections.body:
A minimal CloudFormation template has a small, consistent shape:

```yaml
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Parameters:
  EnvironmentName:
    Type: String
    Default: dev
Resources:
  AppDataBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      BucketName: !Sub 'app-data-${EnvironmentName}'
Outputs:
  BucketArn:
    Value: !GetAtt AppDataBucket.Arn
```

`Parameters` are inputs supplied at deploy time (here `EnvironmentName`, defaulting to `dev`), so one template serves every environment with only the differing values passed in, instead of a near-identical copy per environment. `Resources` declares what should exist. Each entry has a **logical ID** (`AppDataBucket`, the name you use for *this resource* within the template) and a `Type` (`AWS::S3::Bucket`) with `Properties`. The logical ID is not the **physical ID**, the real bucket name AWS assigns or you specify. It is a stable handle within the template that lets other resources reference this one with intrinsic functions like `!Ref` or `!GetAtt` without hardcoding the physical name, so the same template can produce a differently named bucket per environment without changing any wiring. `Outputs` exposes values, here the bucket's ARN, for use outside the template, such as by another stack or a human reading the deploy result.

sections.heading: Stacks, Change Sets, and Why You Review Before You Execute
sections.body:
A **stack** is the deployed, tracked unit that results from applying a template. CloudFormation records which physical resources belong to it, and you change those resources by updating the stack with a modified template instead of working out what to add, remove, or modify yourself. When you propose an update, CloudFormation needn't apply it at once: you can first create a **change set**, a computed preview of what would be added, modified, or removed, without touching anything.

```bash
aws cloudformation create-change-set \
  --stack-name app-network-stack \
  --template-body file://template.yaml \
  --change-set-name widen-db-storage

aws cloudformation describe-change-set \
  --stack-name app-network-stack \
  --change-set-name widen-db-storage
# ... review the Changes array: Action (Add/Modify/Remove), and crucially,
# whether a Modify includes "Replacement": "True"

aws cloudformation execute-change-set \
  --stack-name app-network-stack \
  --change-set-name widen-db-storage
```

This is CloudFormation's equivalent of reviewing a diff before merging. `describe-change-set` shows the planned effect before anyone commits with `execute-change-set`, and the detail to check is whether any `Modify` action carries `"Replacement": "True"`, meaning CloudFormation intends to *delete and recreate* that resource instead of updating it in place. For a stateless resource that is often harmless. For a database or EBS volume, an unnoticed replacement can mean irreversible data loss once the change set runs. That is why reviewing the change set, not just the template diff, matters: some innocent-looking property changes force a replacement, and CloudFormation will tell you in advance if you look. (Two caveats: a change set does not show drift, since it compares templates, and it cannot predict every failure, such as a quota limit hit during execution.)

sections.heading: AWS CDK: Same Engine, a Real Programming Language on Top
sections.body:
**AWS CDK** (Cloud Development Kit) lets you define infrastructure in a general-purpose language (TypeScript, Python, Java, and others) through **constructs**. L1 constructs are thin, generated wrappers that mirror a raw CloudFormation resource type. L2 constructs are hand-written, higher-level abstractions with sensible defaults (an `s3.Bucket` wires up defaults you'd otherwise specify by hand in raw CloudFormation). L3 constructs, called patterns, compose many resources into a ready-made solution to a common problem, such as a load-balanced, autoscaled Fargate service in a few lines.

```python
from aws_cdk import Stack, RemovalPolicy
from aws_cdk import aws_s3 as s3

class DataStack(Stack):
    def __init__(self, scope, construct_id, environment_name, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(scope, construct_id, **kwargs)
        s3.Bucket(
            self, "AppDataBucket",
            bucket_name=f"app-data-{environment_name}",
            removal_policy=RemovalPolicy.RETAIN,
        )
```

Running `cdk synth` compiles code like this into a CloudFormation template: CDK is a code-generation and abstraction layer, not a separate deployment engine. Running `cdk deploy` synthesizes the template and then creates and executes a change set against a stack, as in the raw workflow above, automated behind one command. So everything about stacks, change sets, and replacement risk still applies to CDK-defined infrastructure. Read `cdk diff`, which shows what a deploy would change, as seriously as `describe-change-set` output. CDK is not smarter about safety; it generates the same CloudFormation underneath, with the same risks. (The Python example needs `pip install aws-cdk-lib constructs` and an `app.py` that instantiates `DataStack`; it is a stack definition, not a complete app.)

sections.heading: Common Mistakes: Missing DeletionPolicy, Hardcoded Values, and Silent Replacement
sections.body:
A few recurring mistakes account for many CloudFormation incidents. First, two attributes control what happens to a resource's data. **DeletionPolicy** applies when a resource is removed from the template or its stack is deleted, and **UpdateReplacePolicy** applies when an update replaces the resource. For most resource types both default to `Delete`, so removing a resource from a template (even by accident, through a bad merge or copy-paste error) deletes the real resource at the next stack update. Two exceptions soften this: an S3 bucket that still contains objects can't be deleted, so that deletion fails instead of destroying the data, and `AWS::RDS::DBInstance` (without a `DBClusterIdentifier`) and `AWS::RDS::DBCluster` default `DeletionPolicy` to `Snapshot`. Don't rely on defaults you can't recite. Set `DeletionPolicy: Retain` (or `Snapshot` for resources that support it, such as RDS instances and EBS volumes) on every stateful, important resource, and set `UpdateReplacePolicy` to match so a replacement doesn't discard the old data. Treat it as a checklist item for every stateful resource.

Second, hardcoding a literal account ID in an ARN or a literal Region name makes a template non-portable across accounts and Regions for no benefit. CloudFormation's **pseudo parameters** (`AWS::AccountId`, `AWS::Region`) let a template refer to whichever account and Region it is deployed into. Third, as the change-set discussion showed, some property changes force **replacement** instead of an in-place update, and that isn't always obvious from the template. Changing an RDS instance's `DBInstanceIdentifier` or `StorageEncrypted` setting, or an S3 bucket's name, triggers a delete-and-recreate that a glance at the diff wouldn't flag as dangerous. The change set's `Replacement` flag, not the template diff, is what to check before executing an update to a resource that holds data. (The AWS docs for each resource type list, per property, whether an update needs no interruption, some interruption, or replacement.)

examples.title: A Minimal Template: Parameter, Resource, Output
examples.code:
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09'
Parameters:
  EnvironmentName:
    Type: String
    Default: dev
Resources:
  AppDataBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      BucketName: !Sub 'app-data-${EnvironmentName}'
Outputs:
  BucketArn:
    Value: !GetAtt AppDataBucket.Arn
examples.explanation: `EnvironmentName` is a Parameter, so the same template deploys a differently named bucket per environment (`app-data-dev`, `app-data-staging`, `app-data-prod`) by passing a different value at deploy time, with no duplicated template logic. `AppDataBucket` is the logical ID, how `Outputs` and any other resource in the template refers to this bucket, independent of the physical name `!Sub` produces. `DeletionPolicy: Retain` means removing the resource from the template, or deleting the stack, leaves the real bucket and its data in place, a deliberate safeguard on a resource meant to hold valuable data instead of relying on the default `Delete`. The retained bucket is then no longer managed by any stack, so you must delete it yourself when it's no longer needed. `!GetAtt AppDataBucket.Arn` exposes the ARN for other stacks or a human reading the deploy output, without hardcoding it.

examples.title: Reviewing a Change Set Before Executing It -- Catching a Dangerous Replacement
examples.code:
aws cloudformation create-change-set \
  --stack-name orders-db-stack \
  --template-body file://template.yaml \
  --change-set-name rename-db-instance

aws cloudformation describe-change-set \
  --stack-name orders-db-stack \
  --change-set-name rename-db-instance \
  --query "Changes[].ResourceChange.{Id:LogicalResourceId,Action:Action,Replacement:Replacement}"

# [
#   { "Id": "OrdersDatabase", "Action": "Modify", "Replacement": "True" }
# ]
examples.explanation: The template change looks small, just a new `DBInstanceIdentifier` on an RDS instance, but the change set reports `"Replacement": "True"` for `OrdersDatabase`. CloudFormation intends to create a brand-new database with the new identifier and then delete the old one, not rename it in place. Executing as written would replace the production orders database with an empty one. `UpdateReplacePolicy: Snapshot` would at least preserve a final snapshot of the old instance (the default for replacement is to delete it, with nothing kept). A one-property template diff doesn't show this risk as clearly as the explicit `Replacement` flag, so checking `describe-change-set` output before `execute-change-set` is what catches it.

examples.title: The Same Bucket, Defined With CDK Instead of Raw YAML
examples.code:
from aws_cdk import Stack, RemovalPolicy
from aws_cdk import aws_s3 as s3

class DataStack(Stack):
    def __init__(self, scope, construct_id, environment_name: str, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(scope, construct_id, **kwargs)
        s3.Bucket(
            self, "AppDataBucket",
            bucket_name=f"app-data-{environment_name}",
            removal_policy=RemovalPolicy.RETAIN,
            versioned=True,
            encryption=s3.BucketEncryption.S3_MANAGED,
        )

# cdk synth   -> generates the equivalent CloudFormation template
# cdk diff    -> shows the CDK-level equivalent of a change set, before deploying
# cdk deploy  -> synthesizes, then creates and executes a change set, same as raw CloudFormation
examples.explanation: This produces essentially the same CloudFormation resource as the YAML example, in Python, with `versioned=True` and `encryption=s3.BucketEncryption.S3_MANAGED` added. The L2 construct's typed parameters make these two good practices one-line changes instead of remembering raw property names and enum values. `RemovalPolicy.RETAIN` is CDK's name for the `DeletionPolicy: Retain` in the YAML example: CDK is friendlier vocabulary over the same CloudFormation concepts. `cdk deploy` still goes through the same stack and change-set machinery as the raw `aws cloudformation` commands in the previous example, and `cdk diff` deserves the same careful reading as `describe-change-set`, since it surfaces the same information, including whether a change forces replacement.

misconceptions.description: Running a CloudFormation template a second time with no changes to it will recreate all the resources again.
misconceptions.clarification: CloudFormation is declarative: it compares the template against the stack's current tracked state and computes what differs before doing anything. If the computed change set is empty, CloudFormation does nothing. Templates are safe to reapply, which is what separates a declarative approach from an imperative script that would try to run the same creation commands again.
misconceptions.fact: CloudFormation is declarative: it compares the template against the stack's current tracked state and computes exactly what's different before doing anything.

misconceptions.description: Once a team adopts AWS CDK, CloudFormation's stacks, change sets, and deletion policies are no longer relevant -- CDK replaces them.
misconceptions.clarification: CDK is a code-generation and abstraction layer on top of CloudFormation, not a replacement for its execution engine. `cdk deploy` synthesizes a CloudFormation template and then drives the same stack-and-change-set machinery that `aws cloudformation deploy` would. Stacks tracking resources, change sets previewing updates (including replacement risk), and DeletionPolicy protecting stateful resources all still apply to CDK-defined infrastructure, expressed through CDK's vocabulary (RemovalPolicy, cdk diff) instead of raw template syntax.
misconceptions.fact: CDK is a code-generation and abstraction layer on top of CloudFormation, not a replacement for its execution engine.

exercises.prompt: A change set's describe output shows a single Modify action on an RDS resource with Replacement: True, for a proposed change that turns on storage encryption (StorageEncrypted from false to true). If this change set is executed as-is, and the resource has no UpdateReplacePolicy set (leaving the default), what happens to the database and its data? What should be checked or changed before executing?
exercises.code:
Changes:
  - LogicalResourceId: OrdersDatabase
    Action: Modify
    Replacement: "True"
    Details:
      - Target: { Attribute: Properties, Name: StorageEncrypted, RequiresRecreation: Always }
hints: Replacement: True means CloudFormation plans to delete the existing resource and create a new one, not update the existing one in place.

When an update replaces a resource, the old one is removed under its UpdateReplacePolicy, which defaults to Delete. What does that combination (Replacement + default policy) mean for the existing data?
Before executing, is there a policy setting that would at least preserve a snapshot of the data, rather than losing it outright?
exercises.expectedAnswer: Executing this change set would create a brand-new OrdersDatabase RDS instance with encryption enabled and then delete the original. Because no UpdateReplacePolicy is set, the default Delete applies, so CloudFormation keeps no copy of the original instance's data. Before executing, set UpdateReplacePolicy (and DeletionPolicy) to Snapshot so a final snapshot is taken, or avoid the replacement by another route, such as restoring a snapshot copy into an encrypted instance yourself in a planned migration.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `RequiresRecreation: Always` confirms that `StorageEncrypted` can't be changed in place on this resource type (RDS can't encrypt an existing unencrypted instance), so CloudFormation must create a new instance and delete the old one, which is what `Replacement: True` warns about. The policy that governs this case is `UpdateReplacePolicy`, which defaults to `Delete`, so the old instance and its data would be deleted with nothing preserved automatically. (`DeletionPolicy` covers removal from the template and stack deletion, not replacement, though RDS instances default it to `Snapshot`. Set both.) The safe response is to add `UpdateReplacePolicy: Snapshot` and `DeletionPolicy: Snapshot` before executing, so a final snapshot of the old instance exists. Note the new instance starts empty, so the snapshot still has to be restored or migrated, which is why a planned migration outside the change set is often the better route for a production database. Changing this property is also an example of why the change set, not the template diff, should be read before executing.

exercises.prompt: A template defines an S3 bucket holding financial export files that must never be accidentally deleted. A teammate's recent pull request accidentally removed the bucket's block in a merge conflict resolution, and the change set for that PR shows the bucket as a Remove action. The reviewer almost approved it without noticing. Identify the specific safeguard that was missing from the template itself, and add it.
exercises.code:
Resources:
  FinancialExportsBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      BucketName: financial-exports-prod
      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: Enabled
hints: The bug that caused the near-incident was a bad merge -- but ask what property, if it had been set on this resource from the start, would have changed the OUTCOME even if the same merge mistake happened again.
DeletionPolicy governs what happens to the underlying data when a resource is removed from the template or the stack is deleted -- what's the default for AWS::S3::Bucket if it isn't explicitly set?
Adding the right DeletionPolicy doesn't prevent the merge mistake from happening again, but it changes what that mistake would actually do to the real bucket and its data.
exercises.solutionCode:
Resources:
  FinancialExportsBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    DeletionPolicy: Retain
    Properties:
      BucketName: financial-exports-prod
      VersioningConfiguration:
        Status: Enabled
exercises.solutionExplanation: The template never set `DeletionPolicy` on this bucket, so it relied on the default (`Delete`) for a resource that holds financial data that must never be deleted by accident. (A non-empty bucket can't be deleted, so CloudFormation's delete would likely fail, but that is an accident of the data being present, not a safeguard to rely on: an emptied or lifecycle-expired bucket would go.) Adding `DeletionPolicy: Retain` doesn't stop a bad merge from removing the resource block again and doesn't replace careful review. It does mean that if the resource is removed from the template and the stack updated, CloudFormation keeps the real bucket and its data, turning potential data loss into at worst an orphaned but intact bucket that can be reattached or cleaned up on purpose. Pairing the template safeguard with change-set review, watching for unexpected Remove actions on stateful resources, is the layered defense here; neither alone is enough.

assessments.prompt: A change set's describe output shows an RDS resource with Action: Modify and Replacement: True. What does this specifically indicate, and why does it matter for a stateful resource like a database?
options: Replacement: True is purely informational metadata with no effect on how the update is actually applied.

CloudFormation will update the resource's configuration in place with no downtime or risk to existing data, because replacement here refers only to swapping the template's property values, not the underlying resource.

CloudFormation intends to replace the existing resource with a new one to apply this change, which for a stateful resource can mean data loss unless a policy like UpdateReplacePolicy: Snapshot is set.
The change set has detected an error and will not allow this update to be executed at all.
assessments.explanation: Replacement: True is CloudFormation's signal that a property change cannot be applied to the existing resource in place: it must create a new resource and delete the old one, a far riskier operation than an in-place update for anything stateful, since the new resource starts with no data unless a safeguard such as UpdateReplacePolicy: Snapshot preserves the old one first. The “CloudFormation will update the resource's configuration…” option describes what a Replacement: False modify would mean, not this case. The “The change set has detected an error…” option is incorrect -- CloudFormation will still execute a Replacement: True change set if asked to; it doesn't block it, which is exactly why reviewing this flag before executing matters. The “Replacement: True is purely informational metadata…” option understates its significance -- it's exactly the detail that determines whether an update is safe or potentially destructive for stateful data.

assessments.prompt: A template defines a resource with logical ID AppDataBucket, whose BucketName property is !Sub 'app-data-${EnvironmentName}'. Another resource in the same template references it via !GetAtt AppDataBucket.Arn. If EnvironmentName changes from 'dev' to 'staging' on the next deploy, what happens to that reference?
options: The reference breaks, because the logical ID AppDataBucket must itself be renamed whenever the physical bucket name changes.

Nothing about the reference needs to change -- the logical ID AppDataBucket remains a stable handle within the template regardless of which physical bucket name is actually produced, so !GetAtt continues to resolve correctly to whichever physical bucket the template currently produces.
The reference must be manually rewritten to !GetAtt 'app-data-staging'.Arn to match the new physical bucket name.
CloudFormation requires every reference to a resource to be updated to match its current physical name each time that name changes.
assessments.explanation: A resource's logical ID is a stable identifier within the template itself, entirely independent of whatever physical name the resource is actually given -- that's precisely what lets other parts of the template reference a resource via !Ref or !GetAtt without ever needing to know or hardcode its real, physical name. Changing the parameter that feeds into the physical bucket name has no effect on the logical ID or on references to it. The “The reference breaks, because the logical ID…”, “The reference must be manually rewritten…”, and “CloudFormation requires every reference to a resource…” options all incorrectly assume the reference is tied to the physical name rather than the logical ID, which would defeat the entire purpose of using a stable logical ID as a template-internal handle in the first place.

assessments.prompt: A template hardcodes a literal AWS account ID inside a resource's ARN property instead of using a pseudo parameter. What problem does this most directly create?
options: The template becomes non-portable across accounts -- deploying the identical template into a different AWS account requires manually editing the hardcoded value, whereas AWS::AccountId, a pseudo parameter, would let the same template automatically reference whichever account it's actually deployed into.
Hardcoded account IDs are automatically replaced by CloudFormation with the deploying account's actual ID at deploy time, so there's no real practical problem.
This specifically only matters for templates deployed via CDK; raw CloudFormation templates are unaffected by hardcoded account IDs.
The template will fail validation immediately and refuse to deploy in any AWS account whatsoever.
assessments.explanation: A hardcoded account ID ties the template to one specific account, and reusing that same template in a different account requires manually finding and editing that value -- exactly the kind of per-environment manual edit pseudo parameters like AWS::AccountId are meant to eliminate, letting the same template automatically resolve to whichever account it's actually deployed into. The “The template will fail validation immediately…” option is wrong -- a hardcoded but otherwise valid ARN doesn't fail validation; it deploys successfully, just pointing at the wrong account when reused elsewhere. The “Hardcoded account IDs are automatically replaced…” option invents an automatic substitution CloudFormation does not perform on hardcoded literals. The “This specifically only matters for templates deployed…” option draws an arbitrary distinction -- the portability problem is identical whether the template is authored as raw CloudFormation or synthesized from CDK, since CDK ultimately produces the same underlying template.

assessments.prompt: Explain what AWS CDK actually adds on top of raw CloudFormation, and why someone using CDK still needs to understand stacks, change sets, and DeletionPolicy rather than treating those as CloudFormation-only concerns CDK makes obsolete.
assessments.modelAnswer: CDK adds a real, general-purpose programming language -- and a library of pre-built constructs at increasing levels of abstraction -- as the authoring layer for infrastructure, replacing hand-written YAML or JSON with actual code that can use loops, conditionals, functions, and reusable, testable classes, and that can pull in higher-level constructs (like an L2 S3 bucket construct with sensible secure defaults, or an L3 pattern composing many resources into a ready-made solution) instead of hand-specifying every low-level property. What CDK does not add is a different execution engine underneath: `cdk synth` compiles the CDK code down into an actual CloudFormation template, and `cdk deploy` takes that synthesized template and drives it through the exact same stack-creation and change-set machinery that raw `aws cloudformation` commands use directly. This means every concept that governs how CloudFormation actually applies a change -- a stack tracking which physical resources belong to it, a change set previewing exactly what an update will Add, Modify, or Remove before anything happens (including whether a Modify will actually force a Replacement, deleting and recreating a resource rather than updating it in place), and DeletionPolicy determining whether a resource's underlying data survives being removed from the template or replaced -- applies just as fully to CDK-defined infrastructure as it does to raw templates, just accessed through CDK's own vocabulary (RemovalPolicy instead of DeletionPolicy, cdk diff instead of describe-change-set). Treating CDK as having made these concerns obsolete, rather than simply relabeled and made more ergonomic to configure, is exactly the kind of assumption that would let a dangerous, silent resource replacement slip through a `cdk deploy` just as easily as it could slip through a raw CloudFormation update -- the underlying risk hasn't gone away, only the syntax used to express and guard against it has changed.

concepts.title: How Infrastructure Changes Flow Through a Deployment Pipeline
concepts.description: Infrastructure as code delivers reviewability and reproducibility only if applying it is also a controlled, automated process: a pipeline that reviews a diff, applies it to a lower environment first, and serializes changes against the same environment, instead of engineers running deploy commands from their laptops whenever they like.
learningObjectives: Describe the typical stages an infrastructure change moves through before reaching production: version control, automated plan/diff, human review, apply to a lower environment, promotion to production.
Explain why a pipeline -- rather than an individual engineer's laptop -- should hold the credentials that actually apply infrastructure changes, and how this connects to least privilege.
Explain state locking and why concurrent applies against the same infrastructure can be dangerous.
Explain environment promotion using the same reviewed artifact across dev, staging, and production, and why re-running a manual process separately per environment reintroduces drift risk.
Explain why continuous drift detection remains valuable even alongside a mature, well-run deployment pipeline.

sections.heading: The Shape of a Typical IaC Pipeline
sections.body:
A mature infrastructure change moves through a short, consistent sequence of stages before reaching production. First, an engineer proposes the change as a pull request against the infrastructure code (a CloudFormation template or CDK code), like an application change. Second, a CI job runs a **plan/diff step**, synthesizing the CDK code and running `cdk diff` or creating and describing a CloudFormation change set, and posts the output on the pull request, so the reviewer sees the computed effect of the change and not just source code. Third, a human reviews the diff and approves or requests changes. Fourth, once merged, an automated stage applies the change to a **lower environment** (dev or staging) rather than to production directly. Fifth, after validation there (automated tests, a smoke check, sometimes a deliberate wait), the same reviewed artifact **promotes** to production, typically behind its own approval gate.

This shape closes two gaps from the ClickOps concept: every change that reaches production has already run unmodified against a lower environment, and every change had a computed, reviewable diff before anything executed it. Neither property comes from having infrastructure defined as code. They come from the pipeline that enforces the sequence for every change without relying on anyone to follow it by hand.

sections.heading: Why the Pipeline Holds the Keys, Not a Person's Laptop
sections.body:
An engineer with broad enough IAM permissions can run `cdk deploy` against production from a laptop. That reintroduces the risks a pipeline exists to prevent, even with infrastructure defined as code. No independent review sits between 'the code on this laptop' and 'the change applied to production', since the author is also the executor. Nothing guarantees the laptop's tool versions, dependencies, or uncommitted state match version control, so an uncommitted local tweak could be applied and never reach the reviewed history. And it requires that person to hold broad, standing credentials able to modify production, the long-lived, broadly scoped access the least-privilege discipline from the IAM concept argues against.

The standard practice is for the pipeline's own execution role to be the only identity with permission to apply infrastructure changes, scoped tightly to what deployments need. The CI/CD system assumes it with short-lived federated credentials (GitHub Actions using OIDC to assume an AWS role, or CodePipeline and CodeBuild using their service roles) instead of a long-lived static access key. This gives two benefits: security (no static secret anywhere, and a role no broader than deployments require) and consistency (the applied result is what the pipeline computed from the merged, reviewed commit, not whatever was on one person's laptop with its local tool version and uncommitted changes). In practice, CDK deployments also use a bootstrapped set of roles that `cdk deploy` assumes, so the pipeline role needs permission to assume those roles, not broad resource permissions of its own.

sections.heading: State Locking and the Danger of Concurrent Applies
sections.body:
Infrastructure-as-code tools track the current state of what is deployed so they can compute an accurate plan for the next change. For CloudFormation the stack effectively is that state; other tools, such as Terraform, use an explicit state file (often stored in S3) and take a lock on it before applying. Two applies running concurrently against the same state are dangerous for a mechanical reason: an apply in progress is changing both the real infrastructure and the state describing it, and a second apply that evaluates 'what needs to change' mid-flight computes its plan against state that is about to be stale, and may issue conflicting or overlapping API calls against the same resources.

CloudFormation prevents the narrowest version of this problem itself: a stack has one lifecycle at a time, and if an update is already `UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS`, a second `update-stack` call against that stack is rejected instead of racing the first. The broader lesson goes beyond that built-in protection: applies against the same environment should be serialized, whatever the tool's own locking guarantees. A pipeline enforces this in practice, since a single merge queue feeding a single deploy stage puts only one apply in flight per environment, a guarantee that several engineers running `cdk deploy` from laptops at about the same time don't have. (CI systems provide this as a concurrency group or a serialized environment deployment.)

sections.heading: Environment Promotion: The Same Artifact, Increasing Scrutiny
sections.body:
**Environment promotion** means taking the same reviewed template or synthesized artifact that was just applied and validated in one environment and applying that identical artifact to the next one (dev, then staging, then production), instead of re-running a separate deploy process by hand for each. Differences that must vary (instance sizes, account IDs, a few configuration values) are passed as **parameters** to the same artifact, not kept in separately maintained copies of the logic that drift.

Re-running 'the deploy process' by hand for each environment reopens the drift risk that IaC and pipelines were meant to close. 'Staging's process' and 'production's process', run manually and independently, are two chances to diverge, the ClickOps failure mode moved up a level from console clicks to deploy procedures. A manual approval gate before the production step is still worth keeping, but its purpose is narrower than re-reviewing the change: the diff was reviewed before merge and the artifact was validated in a lower environment, so the gate is a checkpoint for a *business* decision (is now a safe time to deploy this, given everything else going on?), not a second technical review.

sections.heading: Drift Detection as an Ongoing Safety Net, Even With a Good Pipeline
sections.body: A well-run pipeline sharply reduces how often infrastructure diverges from its reviewed source of truth, but not to zero, because the break-glass exception still exists: in a severe incident where the pipeline is unavailable or too slow, a direct out-of-band change is still reasonable. Scheduled drift detection (running `detect-stack-drift` on a recurring schedule, or a drift-monitoring tool across an account's stacks) stays valuable because it catches that residual case, surfaces it as a visible discrepancy, and prompts the backporting discipline covered earlier. It also catches changes you did not expect at all, such as another tool or an automation modifying a resource. Without it, a good pipeline creates a false sense that drift has become impossible.

examples.title: A Pipeline Stage That Posts a Change-Set Diff for Human Review
examples.code:
# Simplified CI pipeline stage (conceptual)
jobs:
  plan:
    steps:
      - checkout: repo
      - run: cdk synth
      - run: cdk diff --app cdk.out > diff-output.txt
      - post-comment:
          target: pull_request
          file: diff-output.txt
  # merging only becomes possible once a human has approved,
  # having actually seen diff-output.txt on the PR

  apply-dev:
    trigger: on_merge_to_main
    steps:
      - run: cdk deploy DevStack --require-approval never

  apply-prod:
    trigger: manual_approval_after(apply-dev)
    steps:
      - run: cdk deploy ProdStack --require-approval never
examples.explanation: The `plan` job runs on every pull request before merge and posts the computed `cdk diff` output as a PR comment, so the reviewer sees what would change if the code were applied instead of guessing from the code alone. `apply-dev` runs after merge and applies the change to a lower environment automatically, with no manual approval since the diff was reviewed before merge. `apply-prod` is gated behind a manual approval available only after `apply-dev` succeeds. That approval isn't a second look at the diff; it confirms this is an appropriate moment for production to receive a change already reviewed and proven in dev. The pipeline syntax is a generic sketch (the keys `post-comment` and `manual_approval_after` are not a real CI system's), so map it onto your CI's own features.

examples.title: Federated, Short-Lived Pipeline Credentials Instead of a Static Access Key
examples.code:
# GitHub Actions job assuming a scoped AWS role via OIDC -- no static access key anywhere
permissions:
  id-token: write
  contents: read

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/GitHubActionsDeployRole
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - run: cdk deploy ProdStack --require-approval never
examples.explanation: `permissions: id-token: write` lets this GitHub Actions job request a short-lived OIDC token, which `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials` exchanges (via `sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`) for temporary AWS credentials for `GitHubActionsDeployRole`. No long-lived IAM user key is generated or stored as a CI secret, which applies the roles-over-static-keys principle from the IAM concept to the pipeline. The role's own permissions policy (not shown) should be scoped to what deployments need, not broad admin for convenience. Its trust policy must also be restricted to your repository and branch or environment through conditions on the token's `sub` claim, or any repository in any GitHub account could try to assume it. That makes the pipeline, not any engineer's standing credentials, the thing that can modify production, with each deployment traceable to a workflow run and a commit.

examples.title: Environment Promotion With Per-Environment Parameters, Same Logic
examples.explanation: Both environments are produced from the same `template.yaml` and the same deploy command; only the supplied parameter file differs, holding the values expected to differ (instance size, capacity bounds) and nothing about architecture or logic. That is 'same artifact, increasing scrutiny': one template is reviewed, tested in dev, and promoted, not two separately maintained templates that look alike today with no guarantee of staying that way. If dev and prod ever need different architecture, treat that deliberately, as an explicit reviewed condition in the template, instead of letting two copies diverge. The template must declare these four parameters, and `deploy` accepts the `file://` form only in the formats its documentation lists, which is why the values sit under a top-level `Parameters` key.

misconceptions.description: Once infrastructure is defined as code, it's safe for any engineer to run cdk deploy or an equivalent command directly from their laptop whenever they want, since the source of truth is the code, not the console.
misconceptions.clarification: Defining infrastructure as code removes the ClickOps risks of no diff and no reproducibility, but applying from a laptop outside a pipeline still skips an independent review-before-apply step (the author applies the change with no gate between), still risks concurrent or conflicting applies with no enforced serialization, and still makes the result depend on that laptop's tool versions and possibly uncommitted state instead of the reviewed, merged commit. A pipeline closes all three gaps, which ad hoc local applies of the same code do not.

misconceptions.description: A mature deployment pipeline with proper review and promotion stages makes drift detection unnecessary, since all changes now go through code review.
misconceptions.clarification: A pipeline enforces process for every change that goes through it, but it doesn't eliminate the break-glass exception: an incident severe enough that a direct, out-of-band console change is the right call. Periodic drift detection remains necessary to catch those cases and prompt backporting, instead of assuming good process on the normal path guarantees deployed reality can never diverge from the reviewed template.
misconceptions.fact: A pipeline enforces process for every change that goes through it, but it doesn't eliminate the legitimate break-glass exception -- an incident severe enough that a direct, out-of-band console change is still the right call in the moment.

exercises.prompt: A team's CI pipeline is configured so that merging any pull request to main immediately runs `cdk deploy` against the production account, using a long-lived IAM user access key stored as a CI secret, with no lower-environment deploy step and no approval gate before the production apply. A bad change reached production within two minutes of merge, with no chance for anyone to catch it before real impact. Identify the specific pipeline design problems and describe the fixes.
exercises.code:
# current pipeline (simplified)
on: push to main
jobs:
  deploy:
    steps:
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          aws-access-key-id: ${{ secrets.PROD_AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }}
          aws-secret-access-key: ${{ secrets.PROD_AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }}
      - run: cdk deploy ProdStack --require-approval never
hints: Count the stages between 'merged to main' and 'applied to production' -- is there a lower-environment deploy step, or a plan/diff review, or an approval gate anywhere in this sequence at all?
Look at how credentials are supplied to this job -- is this a long-lived static secret, or something short-lived and scoped specifically to this pipeline's own identity?
Consider each fix independently: what changes about the review/promotion flow, and separately, what changes about how credentials are obtained.
exercises.solutionCode:
on: push to main
jobs:
  apply-dev:
    steps:
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/GitHubActionsDeployRole
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - run: cdk diff DevStack   # posted/reviewed as part of the originating PR, before merge
      - run: cdk deploy DevStack --require-approval never

  apply-prod:
    needs: apply-dev
    environment:
      name: production   # requires a configured manual approval gate
    steps:
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v4
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::444455556666:role/GitHubActionsDeployRole
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - run: cdk deploy ProdStack --require-approval never
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original pipeline had two compounding problems. First, it went from merge straight to a production apply, with no lower-environment validation and no approval gate, so a change that a few minutes in dev or a human sign-off would have caught reached real users within two minutes. The fix splits it into an `apply-dev` stage that runs on merge (the diff having been reviewed on the pull request beforehand) and an `apply-prod` stage that depends on `apply-dev` succeeding and sits behind an environment-level manual approval. Second, it authenticated with a long-lived IAM user access key stored as a CI secret, a standing credential that stays dangerous indefinitely if it leaks from the CI system. The fix uses OIDC role assumption, giving short-lived credentials scoped to a deployment role, with no static secret stored. (The solution YAML is abbreviated: a real workflow also needs `permissions: id-token: write`, a checkout step, and `cdk` installed.)

exercises.prompt: Two engineers, at nearly the same moment, each run `cdk deploy AppStack` from their own laptops against the same CloudFormation stack, unaware the other is doing the same thing. Predict what CloudFormation does, and explain why a pipeline with a single merge queue avoids this scenario entirely.
exercises.code:
# Engineer A's terminal, 10:03:00
$ cdk deploy AppStack

# Engineer B's terminal, 10:03:02 (two seconds later)
$ cdk deploy AppStack
hints: CloudFormation tracks a stack's status (e.g. UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS) -- what does it do if a second update-stack call arrives while a stack is already in that status?

One of the two deploys will very likely succeed in starting first -- think about what happens to the other one specifically because of that stack-level status check, not because of anything either engineer did wrong.

Consider what property of a CI pipeline (specifically, how many applies against the same environment it allows to be in flight simultaneously) prevents this race from being possible at all, rather than merely handling it gracefully after the fact.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Whichever cdk deploy actually issues its update-stack call first (say, Engineer A's) transitions the stack into UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS. Engineer B's nearly-simultaneous update-stack call against the same stack is rejected by CloudFormation, since a stack only supports one update lifecycle at a time -- Engineer B's deploy fails outright rather than racing or corrupting anything. A pipeline avoids this scenario entirely (rather than just handling it safely after the fact) because a single merge queue feeding a single deploy stage means only one apply against a given environment is ever triggered at a time in the first place -- there's no possibility of two applies being kicked off concurrently to begin with.
exercises.solutionExplanation: CloudFormation's stack-level protection means this race doesn't corrupt anything: only one update can be in progress per stack, and a second concurrent attempt is rejected, so the rejected engineer retries once the first finishes. It is a real safety net but a reactive one. It prevents damage, yet the race, the wasted attempt, the confusing error, and the question of who retries still happen. A pipeline with a single merge queue removes the precondition: merges and the deploys they trigger are processed one at a time, so two applies against the same environment can't be triggered concurrently at all, a stronger guarantee than 'concurrent applies are handled safely if they happen'.

assessments.prompt: A pipeline deploys directly to production on every merge to main, with no lower-environment deploy step and no approval gate. Which change most directly addresses the biggest structural risk in this setup?
options: Require every pull request to have at least two reviewer approvals before merge.
Switch the pipeline's credentials from a static IAM user access key to a federated, short-lived role, leaving the rest of the flow unchanged, so that no long-lived secret remains in the pipeline.
Add more detailed logging to the deploy step so failures are easier to diagnose after they happen in production.
Add a lower-environment (e.g. dev or staging) deploy stage that runs first, followed by a required manual approval gate specifically before the production deploy stage.
assessments.explanation: The structural risk is that every merged change reaches production immediately, with no validation in a lower environment and no human checkpoint before real impact, which a lower-environment stage and a production approval gate address directly. Improving credential handling (“Switch the pipeline's credentials from a static…”) is a good, separate improvement that matches least-privilege practice, but it doesn't address the missing validation and approval sequence: a change deployed with short-lived credentials still reaches production immediately. More PR reviewers (“Require every pull request to have…”) strengthens the pre-merge review but doesn't address what happens after merge, which is where this specific risk lives. Better logging (“Add more detailed logging to the deploy…”) only helps diagnose a problem after it has already reached production, rather than reducing the chance production is reached with a bad change in the first place.

assessments.prompt: Two engineers each run cdk deploy AppStack against the same stack within two seconds of each other, unaware the other is doing the same thing. What does CloudFormation actually do?
options: Both updates are automatically merged together into a single combined change.
CloudFormation pauses the second engineer's deploy indefinitely until someone manually cancels the first one.
Both updates proceed concurrently against the stack, and CloudFormation applies whichever one happens to finish last as the final state.
Whichever call arrives first moves the stack into UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS; the second update is rejected outright.
assessments.explanation: CloudFormation tracks a single lifecycle status per stack, and once a stack is UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS, a second update call against it is rejected instead of racing the first. It is a real built-in safety net, though a reactive one: the rejected engineer has to retry after the first update completes. The “Both updates are automatically merged together into…” option invents a merge behavior CloudFormation does not perform. The “Both updates proceed concurrently against the stack…” option describes exactly the dangerous race this protection exists to prevent. The “CloudFormation pauses the second engineer's deploy indefinitely…” option fabricates an indefinite pause requiring manual cancellation, which isn't how the rejection behaves -- it fails immediately rather than waiting.

assessments.prompt: A team argues that since their deployment pipeline enforces code review and lower-environment validation for every change, periodic drift detection is now redundant and can be turned off entirely. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: There is no flaw; a mature pipeline structurally guarantees that deployed infrastructure can never diverge from its reviewed template.

A pipeline enforces process for every change that goes through it, but it doesn't eliminate the legitimate break-glass exception -- a severe incident where the pipeline itself is unavailable or too slow can still justify a direct, out-of-band change; drift detection remains valuable specifically to catch and prompt backporting of exactly those residual cases.
Drift detection is genuinely redundant, because CloudFormation change sets already perform the equivalent of drift detection before every pipeline-driven apply.
Drift detection was only ever useful for accounts that don't use CDK, so a CDK-based pipeline makes it unnecessary regardless of process maturity.
assessments.explanation: A good pipeline sharply reduces how often infrastructure diverges from its source of truth, but it governs only the changes that flow through it. It has no bearing on a break-glass emergency where the pipeline is unavailable or too slow, the residual case drift detection exists to catch. The “There is no flaw; a mature pipeline…” option overstates the pipeline's guarantee to an absolute that the reasoning explicitly rejects. The “Drift detection is genuinely redundant, because CloudFormation…” option confuses change sets (which preview a specific pipeline-initiated change before applying it) with drift detection (which checks whether reality has already diverged from the template via some other path) -- they serve different purposes. The “Drift detection was only ever useful…” option draws an arbitrary, unsupported distinction between CDK and non-CDK pipelines; the break-glass risk applies identically to both, since both ultimately drive the same underlying CloudFormation stacks.

assessments.prompt: Explain why a deployment pipeline -- not an individual engineer's laptop -- should be the thing that actually holds credentials and applies infrastructure changes, even when the infrastructure is already fully defined as reviewed, version-controlled code.
assessments.modelAnswer: Defining infrastructure as code solves the ClickOps problems of no diff and no reproducibility, but it doesn't guarantee that the reviewed code is the code that gets applied, or that applies are safe with respect to each other. Both depend on how the code is executed. If an engineer runs the deploy command from a laptop, several gaps reopen even though the template or CDK code is fine. There is no independent checkpoint between writing and applying the change, and nothing forces a review to have happened or to match what is about to run, as opposed to a locally modified or uncommitted version. Nothing serializes that apply against another engineer's concurrent one. And the credentials are typically the individual's standing, broadly scoped access, the kind least privilege argues against for routine operations, instead of a role scoped to a deployment and assumed only for its duration. A pipeline closes all three gaps together: it drives the apply from exactly the merged, reviewed commit (not a local working copy that might differ from what anyone reviewed), it naturally serializes applies against a given environment through its own merge queue and deploy sequencing, and it authenticates using its own scoped, typically federated and short-lived credentials rather than any individual's personal access. None of this distrusts the engineer's competence. It is the same reasoning as requiring code review even for a strong engineer: the value comes from a structural guarantee that holds whoever is involved.
